q: What is the mean of 4, 8, 6, 10, 7?
x: Sum = 4 + 8 + 6 + 10 + 7 = 35, and 35 / 5 = 7. 35 is the sum before dividing by the number of values.

q: What is the median of 12, 4, 9, 2, 15, 6?
x: Sorted: 2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 15. With 6 values the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th: (6 + 9) / 2 = 7.5. Taking the middle two without sorting (9 and 2) gives 5.5; 8 is the mean (48 / 6).

q: What is the mode of 3, 5, 7, 5, 2, 7, 5, 9?
x: The mode is the most frequent value: 5 appears three times, 7 twice, the others once. So the mode is 5, not 7.

q: What is the range of 14, 3, 22, 9, 17?
x: Range = largest − smallest = 22 − 3 = 19. 22 is just the largest value; 25 adds instead of subtracting.

q: Data: 5, 6, 7, 8, 94. Which value best describes a typical value of this set?
o: The mean, 24
The median, 7
The range, 89
The mean, 7
x: Mean = 120 / 5 = 24, pulled up by the outlier 94; the median (middle of the sorted values) is 7 and is not affected by it. The range, 94 − 5 = 89, measures spread, not a typical value.

q: The mean of 5 numbers is 12. A sixth number, 18, is added. What is the new mean?
x: The 5 numbers total 5 × 12 = 60; with 18 the total is 78, and 78 / 6 = 13. 15 comes from wrongly averaging 12 and 18.

q:
What is printed?
```
data = [4, 7, 7, 10, 12]
print(sum(data) / len(data))
```
x: sum(data) = 4 + 7 + 7 + 10 + 12 = 40 and len(data) = 5. In Python 3, `/` always gives a float, so 40 / 5 prints `8.0`, not `8`.

q:
What is printed?
```
data = [9, 2, 7, 4, 6]
data.sort()
mid = len(data) // 2
print(data[mid])
```
x: After sorting, data = [2, 4, 6, 7, 9]; mid = 5 // 2 = 2, and data[2] = 6, the median. 7 is the item at index 2 before sorting; 5.6 is the mean (28 / 5).

q: Set P: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Set Q: 28, 29, 30, 31, 32. Which statement is true?
o: Both have mean 30, but P has the larger range
P has the larger mean and the larger range
Both have the same mean and the same range
Q has the larger range because its values are closer together
x: Mean of P = 150 / 5 = 30 and mean of Q = 150 / 5 = 30. Range of P = 50 − 10 = 40, range of Q = 32 − 28 = 4, so P is more spread out.

q: A model is tested on 25 new cases and predicts 20 of them correctly. What is its accuracy?
x: Accuracy = correct / total = 20 / 25 = 0.8 = 80%. 125% comes from dividing the wrong way (25 / 20).

q: A spam filter is tested on 50 emails. It correctly marks 18 spam emails as spam and correctly passes 24 normal emails; the rest are wrong. What is its accuracy?
x: Correct predictions = 18 + 24 = 42, so accuracy = 42 / 50 = 84%. 36% counts only the correct spam (18 / 50) and 16% is the error rate (8 / 50).

q: Why is a model evaluated on test data that was not used to build (train) it?
o: To check how well it works on new, unseen data
To make the training faster
Because test data never has errors
To increase the size of the training data
x: A model can fit its training data well yet fail on new cases, so it is judged on separate test data. Keeping test data apart does not speed training or enlarge the training set.

q: Descriptive statistics are used to
o: prove that a hypothesis is true
collect new data from users
predict exact future values without any data
summarise the main features of a data set, such as its centre and spread
x: Descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, range and similar) summarise data already collected. They do not prove hypotheses; hypothesis testing only gives evidence for or against H₀.

q: To test whether a revision app raises scores, one group of students uses the app and a similar group studies without it. The group without the app is the
o: experimental group
dependent group
outlier group
control group
x: The control group does not get the treatment and is used for comparison. The group that uses the app is the experimental group.

q: A researcher changes the number of practice hours given to students and measures their test scores. The test score is the
o: independent variable
dependent variable
control group
sample size
x: The variable the researcher changes (practice hours) is the independent variable; the one measured to see the effect (test score) is the dependent variable.

q: What is true about the mode of 6, 2, 8, 2, 8, 5, 3?
o: It has one mode, 8
It has one mode, 2
It has no mode
It has two modes, 2 and 8
x: 2 appears twice and 8 appears twice, while 6, 5 and 3 appear once, so the data has two modes (bimodal). Choosing only one of them misses the tie.

q: Which order of steps fits a typical data-science workflow?
o: Clean data → collect data → visualise → analyse
Visualise → collect data → clean data → analyse
Analyse → clean data → collect data → share results
Collect data → clean data → analyse data → visualise and share results
x: Data must be collected before it can be cleaned, and cleaned before it is analysed; results are then shown and shared. Cleaning cannot come before there is data to clean.

q: Which of these is a data-cleaning step?
o: Drawing a pie chart of the results
Removing duplicate rows and handling missing values
Writing the null hypothesis
Presenting findings to the manager
x: Cleaning prepares raw data for analysis: removing duplicates, filling or removing missing values and correcting errors. Charts and presentations come later, in visualisation and communication.

q: A column of student ages reads 17, 18, (blank), 19, 250. Which two problems should data cleaning deal with?
o: A missing value and an impossible value
A duplicate row and a missing value
Two impossible values
A text value and a duplicate row
x: The blank is a missing value and 250 cannot be a student's age, so it is an impossible (invalid) value. No value is repeated, so there is no duplicate.

q: Which chart best shows how a city's average temperature changes over the 12 months of a year?
o: Pie chart
Line chart
Scatter plot
Histogram
x: A line chart joins values in time order, so rises and falls across the months are easy to see. A pie chart shows parts of a whole, and months' temperatures are not parts of a total.

q: Which chart best shows what share (percentage) of a family's monthly budget goes to food, rent, transport and savings?
o: Line chart
Scatter plot
Pie chart
Histogram
x: A pie chart shows how a whole (the budget) is divided into parts. A line chart is for change over time, which is not asked here.

q: Which chart best shows whether students who study more hours tend to get higher marks?
o: Pie chart
Histogram of marks only
Bar chart of the class's total marks
Scatter plot
x: A scatter plot puts each student as a point (hours, marks), showing the relationship between two numeric variables. A histogram of marks alone ignores hours studied.

q: In a data set, the City column contains "Lahore", "lahore" and "LAHORE " (with a trailing space). Counting rows per city shows three different cities instead of one. Which cleaning step fixes this?
o: Standardise the text: use the same letter case and trim extra spaces
Delete every row that mentions Lahore
Fill the City column's blanks with the mean
Draw a bar chart of the three spellings
x: The three values differ only in case and spacing, so making the format consistent turns them into one city. Deleting the rows loses data, and a mean cannot be taken of text.

q: In hypothesis testing, the null hypothesis (H₀) usually states that
o: there is an effect or a difference
the sample was collected wrongly
the p-value is less than 0.05
there is no effect or no difference
x: H₀ is the 'nothing new' statement: no effect, no difference. The claim of an effect or difference is the alternative hypothesis H₁.

q: Research question: does a new teaching method change students' average score? Which pair of hypotheses is correct?
o: H₀: the method makes no difference to the average score; H₁: the method changes the average score
H₀: the method changes the average score; H₁: the method makes no difference to the average score
H₀: the method raises scores by 10 marks; H₁: the method lowers scores
H₀ and H₁ both: the method changes the average score
x: H₀ states no difference, and H₁ states the effect the researcher is looking for (a change). Swapping them is the common mistake.

q: A test gives p = 0.03 with significance level α = 0.05. What is the decision?
o: Do not reject H₀
Reject H₁ and keep H₀
Reject H₀
Repeat the test until p > 0.05
x: The rule is to reject H₀ when p < α; 0.03 < 0.05, so H₀ is rejected. Not rejecting would be right only if p were 0.05 or more.

q: A test gives p = 0.12 with α = 0.05. What is the correct decision?
o: Reject H₀ and accept H₁
Reject both H₀ and H₁
Do not reject H₀ (there is not enough evidence against it)
Raise α to 0.15 so that H₀ can be rejected
x: 0.12 is not less than 0.05, so H₀ is not rejected. α is fixed before the test; raising it afterwards to get a rejection is not allowed.

q: A study finds p = 0.03. Which statement is correct?
o: H₀ is rejected at α = 0.01 but not at α = 0.05
H₀ is rejected at both α = 0.05 and α = 0.01
H₀ is rejected at α = 0.05 but not at α = 0.01
H₀ is rejected at neither α = 0.05 nor α = 0.01
x: Reject H₀ when p < α: 0.03 < 0.05, so reject at 0.05; 0.03 is not below 0.01, so do not reject at 0.01. A smaller α needs stronger evidence.

q: In hypothesis testing, the significance level α (for example 0.05) is
o: the probability that H₁ is true
the cut-off chosen before the test: reject H₀ when the p-value is below it
the average of the sample data
the number of observations in the sample
x: α is the threshold set in advance; the p-value from the data is compared with it. It is not the chance that H₁ is true.

q: A company claims its phone's battery lasts more than 10 hours on average. A researcher tests this claim. Which pair of hypotheses fits?
o: H₀: mean battery life > 10 hours; H₁: mean battery life = 10 hours
H₀: mean battery life < 10 hours; H₁: mean battery life > 10 hours
H₀: mean battery life = 10 hours; H₁: mean battery life > 10 hours
H₀: mean battery life ≠ 10 hours; H₁: mean battery life = 10 hours
x: The claim to be supported ('more than 10') is H₁, and H₀ is the no-effect value, 10 hours. Putting the claim in H₀ reverses the roles; H₀ must contain the equality.
